To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) viewing images of food can trigger neural activity in the reward system; 2) viewing images of highly palatable foods can increase the desire for such foods and trigger physiological responses (such as salivation) that are consistent with a desire to consume; and 3) viewing images of desirable foods increases visual attention towards food cues in the environment, which may increase exposure to food cues, and thus the likelihood of eating.

(1) viewing food pictures, especially when hungry, activates the same brain regions as actually tasting the food, (2) the more we view food pictures, the more we like the taste of the food we are eating, (3) viewing pictures of food increases the desire to eat, and (4) viewing food pictures increases the likelihood of overeating, and of eating more unhealthy food, and of choosing more unhealthy foods in the future.

viewing food images increases neural activity in brain regions associated with reward processing and hunger, and that this is accompanied by physiological and psychological changes, including increases in hunger, desire to eat, and salivation.
